    Pyrifos: Correlated Random Intercepts and Slopes

    pyrifos-random-slope.Rmd

    Phase 27 supports one deliberately narrow random-slope design: a balanced, complete two-condition comparison with a correlated random intercept and slope for each subject. In vegan::pyrifos, the 12 experimental ditches are subjects. We compare an early post-treatment period (weeks 1 and 2) with a later period (weeks 4 and 8), using the two dates within each period as replicated community observations.

    Build complete ditch-period cells 

    ditch <- gl(12, 1, length = 132)
week <- factor(rep(c(-4, -1, 0.1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 15, 19, 24), each = 12))
keep <- week %in% c(1, 2, 4, 8)

community <- pyrifos[keep, ]
environment <- data.frame(
  ditch = droplevels(ditch[keep]),
  week = droplevels(week[keep]),
  period = factor(
    ifelse(week[keep] %in% c(1, 2), "early", "late"),
    levels = c("early", "late")
  )
)
with(environment, table(ditch, period))
#>      period
#> ditch early late
#>    1      2    2
#>    2      2    2
#>    3      2    2
#>    4      2    2
#>    5      2    2
#>    6      2    2
#>    7      2    2
#>    8      2    2
#>    9      2    2
#>    10     2    2
#>    11     2    2
#>    12     2    2

    Every ditch contributes two early and two late observations. The random-slope formula is explicit: the intercept is the ditch midpoint across periods, and the slope is the complete late - early community-difference vector.

    design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ period + (1 + period | ditch),
  environment,
  vegdist(community, method = "bray")
)
design$random_term_table
#>             term origin parent variables         expression  slope correlated
#> 1 1+period|ditch  slope   <NA>     ditch 1 + period | ditch period       TRUE

    Test the population mean change

    The numerator is the squared norm of the mean ditch difference. Its denominator is variation among ditch difference vectors. Whole difference vectors receive independent sign flips; observations, dates, and individual community coordinates are never permuted separately.

    fit <- permanova_random_slope(
  design,
  permutations = "all",
  keep_permutations = TRUE,
  truncate = TRUE
)
fit$table
#>                           term df        ss         ms pseudo_f       p_sign
#> 1                       period  1 0.4241459 0.42414594 6.790503 0.0004882812
#> 2 Between-subject random slope 11 0.6870780 0.06246164       NA           NA
#>   p_parametric
#> 1           NA
#> 2           NA
fit$test[c(
  "hypothesis", "estimand", "exchangeability_units",
  "exchangeability_assumption", "attainable_permutations",
  "exact_permutation"
)]
#> $hypothesis
#> [1] "the population mean subject difference `late - early` is zero"
#> 
#> $estimand
#> [1] "equally weighted complete-subject condition-difference vectors"
#> 
#> $<NA>
#> NULL
#> 
#> $exchangeability_assumption
#> [1] "central symmetry of subject difference vectors under the fixed-effect null"
#> 
#> $attainable_permutations
#> [1] 4096
#> 
#> $exact_permutation
#> [1] TRUE

    With 12 ditches, all 2^12 = 4096 sign assignments are attainable. Calling this exact refers to the declared central-symmetry model: under the fixed-effect null, each complete ditch difference vector must have the same distribution as its negative. Weeks were not randomized to early and late labels, so this is a population symmetry analysis, not a causal randomization test of calendar time.

    Inspect the covariance model

    The distance engine reports trace covariance components for the centred ditch midpoint and the late-minus-early slope. Equal within-cell sampling noise is removed by method of moments. Negative unrestricted components remain visible; the positive-semidefinite truncation is a separate sensitivity.

    fit$covariance$parameterization
#> [1] "random intercept is the midpoint of `early` and `late`; random slope is `late - early`"
fit$covariance$unrestricted
#>                  random_intercept random_slope
#> random_intercept      0.053054141  0.003876849
#> random_slope          0.003876849  0.015518980
fit$covariance$truncated
#>                  random_intercept random_slope
#> random_intercept      0.053054141  0.003876849
#> random_slope          0.003876849  0.015518980
fit$covariance$intercept_slope_correlation
#> [1] 0.1351101

    For a Euclidean scalar response, the fixed-effect pseudo-F is exactly the squared paired t statistic, and the covariance matrix is the usual residual-corrected covariance of subject midpoints and differences. For non-Euclidean dissimilarities the complete signed spectrum remains in the empirical sign-flip analysis, while the Gaussian parametric p-value is suppressed.

    Know the boundary

    Phase 27 rejects more than two conditions, incomplete subjects, unequal or unreplicated subject-condition cells, additional fixed terms, multiple random slopes, and numerically zero between-subject slope variation. A multi-level time factor would require a defensible covariance-specific multivariate test; it is not treated as though a single repeated-measures denominator implied sphericity.
